prompt: What does an AMI actually hold?
hint: Where are the bytes of the disk?

choices.text: The disk itself, as one image file uploaded to S3
choices.why: The bytes are in snapshots. The AMI is the record that names them.

choices.text: The operating system's name and version
choices.why: It carries far more: architecture, boot mode, root device and the block device mapping.

choices.text: A stopped instance, kept so that it can be cloned
choices.why: An AMI is made from an instance, but it is not one, and nothing in it is running or stopped.

choices.text: A record of the machine, naming snapshots
choices.why: Right. A launch makes a volume from each snapshot in the mapping.

prompt: Why read /aws/service/ami-amazon-linux-latest/al2023-ami-kernel-default-x86_64 instead of writing the AMI id into a template?
hint: What happens to the id every few weeks?

choices.text: The name stays put while the id changes
choices.why: Right. The parameter moves and the template that reads it does not.

choices.text: The parameter is cheaper to read than describe-images
choices.why: Cost has nothing to do with it; both reads are free.

choices.text: An AMI id cannot be written into a launch template
choices.why: It can; it is simply a fact that stops being true.

choices.text: The id is secret and only the parameter is public
choices.why: Public image ids are visible to everybody through describe-images.

prompt: An old script finds Ubuntu with describe-images, a name filter of ubuntu/images/* and no --owners. What is the risk on AWS?
hint: Who may publish a public image?

choices.text: It matches nothing, because a name filter needs an owner
choices.why: A name filter works alone; that is the problem.

choices.text: It sorts by CreationDate wrongly, as it did in moto
choices.why: That is moto's dating. On AWS the date is real and the sort works.

choices.text: It matches impostors' public images of that name
choices.why: Right. Only the owner id says Canonical made it.

choices.text: It returns images from every region at once
choices.why: describe-images answers for one region, the one you are in.

prompt: The part of an AMI that becomes the new instance's disks is its block device ___.
In moto's record of the Amazon Linux 2023 image, which values are moto's rather than AWS's? Choose all that apply.

choices.text: A CreationDate of the moment moto started
choices.why: moto dates every image it ships that way.

choices.text: A 15 GB root of type standard
choices.why: AWS's record maps an 8 GiB gp3 root.

choices.text: DeleteOnTermination false on the root
choices.why: AWS's image deletes its root with the instance.

choices.text: Architecture x86_64
choices.why: The name says x86_64 and so does AWS.
That is Amazon's account, in moto and on AWS.

prompt: A volume already has one snapshot. What does the second snapshot of it store?

choices.text: Only the blocks that changed since the first
choices.why: Right, and it points back at the first for the rest.

choices.text: Every block of the volume again, so that it stands alone
choices.why: It stands alone without storing them again: AWS keeps the blocks it refers to.

choices.text: The files that changed, as a list of paths
choices.why: A snapshot knows blocks, not files.

choices.text: No blocks yet; they are copied when the first is deleted
choices.why: It stores its changed blocks the moment it is taken.

prompt: A volume has 80 GB written. A nightly snapshot is kept for 30 days and 2 GB change each day. At 0.068 USD per GB-month, what do the 30 snapshots cost a month, in USD?
hint: The first stores what was written; each of the other 29 stores a day's change.

prompt: Monday's snapshot is deleted. What happens to Tuesday's, which referred to Monday's for most of its blocks?

choices.text: It is damaged, and can no longer be restored
choices.why: AWS never frees a block a later snapshot still needs.

choices.text: AWS refuses to delete Monday's while Tuesday's exists
choices.why: Any snapshot in a chain may be deleted. What refuses is a snapshot used by a registered AMI.

choices.text: It is still whole: every block it needed is kept
choices.why: Right. Only what was unique to Monday's is freed.

choices.text: It becomes a full copy and its price doubles
choices.why: The bill falls by what was unique to Monday's; nothing is copied.

prompt: describe-snapshots shows VolumeSize 100 for both snapshots. What is that number?

choices.text: What each snapshot stores, in GB
choices.why: What a snapshot stores is never printed there; it shows on the bill.

choices.text: The size of the volume the snapshot was taken from
choices.why: Right. It is the same for every snapshot of that volume.

choices.text: The percentage of the volume that has been copied so far
choices.why: That is Progress, a different field.

choices.text: moto's placeholder for a price in cents
choices.why: No price appears in a snapshot's record, in moto or on AWS.

prompt: A data volume in sa-east-1a has to be used by an instance in sa-east-1c. How is it moved?
hint: A volume never leaves its zone; a snapshot belongs to the region.

choices.text: modify-volume, naming the new zone
choices.why: modify-volume changes size, type and performance, never the zone.

choices.text: copy-snapshot into sa-east-1c first, then create the volume there
choices.why: copy-snapshot copies between regions. Inside one region the snapshot is already usable in every zone.

choices.text: Attach it to the instance in sa-east-1c and let AWS move it
choices.why: AWS refuses to attach a volume to an instance in another zone; lesson 3 shows moto does not.

choices.text: Snapshot it, then create a volume from the snapshot in sa-east-1c
choices.why: Right. The new volume is a separate one; the old can then be deleted.

prompt: moto made a 50 GB volume from a snapshot of a 100 GB volume. What does AWS do with that request?

choices.text: It creates it and drops the blocks past 50 GB
choices.why: AWS never truncates a disk; it refuses the size.

choices.text: It creates it if only 50 GB were written
choices.why: What was written does not matter; the volume size does.

choices.text: It creates it and shrinks the file system to fit
choices.why: EBS does not touch the file system; it sees blocks.

choices.text: It refuses every smaller size
choices.why: Right. Shrinking is done inside the operating system, by copying files.

prompt: Put the steps of building an image of your own in order.
hint: The image captures the instance at the moment it is made.
items: Launch an instance from a published image
Run create-image, which reboots it and snapshots its volumes
Launch the machines from the new AMI id
trap: Running create-image before configuring captures the base image unchanged, with a new id.

prompt: What does create-image do to the instance by default, before it takes the snapshots?

choices.text: Terminates it, since its job is done
choices.why: The instance survives; Packer terminates its own builder instance, create-image does not.

choices.text: Stops it, and leaves it stopped
choices.why: It comes back up; a reboot is not a stop.

choices.text: Reboots it, so the file system is at rest
choices.why: Right. Without it the image has the consistency of a power cut.

choices.text: Nothing at all: the snapshot is taken while the instance runs, with every write since the boot still in memory
choices.why: That is what --no-reboot asks for, and it is not the default.

prompt: A database password was written into an image, which is then shared with two other accounts. What follows?
hint: Where do the image's bytes end up?

choices.text: Nothing, because a shared image is read-only
choices.why: Read-only still means readable: a launched instance has the whole disk.

choices.text: Anyone launching it can read the password
choices.why: Right. It is in every snapshot and every launch; fetch secrets at boot instead.

choices.text: The password is removed automatically when the image is shared
choices.why: EC2 knows nothing about the files on the disk.

choices.text: Only the owner's account can read it, because the snapshots stay private
choices.why: The other account launches volumes made from those snapshots, and reads them.

prompt: Match each name to what it is.
hint: Two tools, a flag, a field, a habit.

pairs.right: AWS's managed pipeline of recipes and components
A builder that launches, provisions and calls create-image
An image with the consistency of a power cut
The instance an image was made from
The standard image a team's machines start from

right_distractors: The date an image stops being listed

prompt: An image does not change after it is made, so a fix is a new image with a new ___.
An image is deregistered. What happens to the snapshot its mapping named?
hint: AWS cannot know whether you meant to keep it.

choices.text: It always stays, billed until somebody deletes it
choices.why: Right. Deregistering removes the record and leaves the blocks.

choices.text: It is deleted together with the image
choices.why: That is the half-right picture: the record goes and the blocks stay.

choices.text: It moves to an archive tier for free
choices.why: Nothing moves on its own, and no tier is free.

choices.text: It becomes public, since it has no image left
choices.why: A snapshot keeps its own permissions; it stays private.

prompt: An account has 200 deregistered images whose 15 GB snapshots were never deleted, each stored whole. At 0.068 USD per GB-month, what do they cost a month, in USD?
delete-snapshot on the snapshot of a registered image: what answers, in moto and on AWS?

choices.text: A refusal, InvalidSnapshot.InUse
choices.why: Right. The image goes first, then the snapshot.

choices.text: The snapshot is deleted and the image is left with no disk
choices.why: That is exactly what the refusal prevents.

choices.text: The image is deregistered along with it
choices.why: Neither deregisters anything on its own.

choices.text: moto refuses it, and AWS deletes it
choices.why: Both refuse; this is one place moto checks what AWS checks.

prompt: An image's deprecation date has passed. What does that change on AWS?
hint: Nothing that depends on it breaks on the day.

choices.text: It is deregistered and its snapshots are deleted
choices.why: Deprecation removes nothing; deregistering is a separate act.

choices.text: Other accounts stop finding it in listings, and it still launches by id
choices.why: Right. New users stop finding it; existing ones keep working.

choices.text: Every launch of it fails with an error that names the date that passed
choices.why: It still launches for anybody who has the id.

choices.text: Running instances made from it are stopped
choices.why: Nothing running is touched.

prompt: An image encrypted with the default AWS-managed EBS key has to be launched from another account. What works?
hint: That key is private to its account.

choices.text: A launch permission naming the other account, as for any image
choices.why: The permission is granted, and the launch still fails: the other account cannot use the key.

choices.text: Making the image public, which bypasses the key
choices.why: An encrypted image cannot be made public, and publishing an image is its own risk.

choices.text: Copy it under a customer-managed KMS key whose policy lets them use it, and share the copy
choices.why: Right. The copy is the moment to choose the key.

choices.text: Nothing: encrypted images can never leave their account
choices.why: They can, with a key the other account is allowed to use.

prompt: An image is copied from sa-east-1 to us-east-1. Which of these are true? Choose all that apply.

choices.text: The copy has an id of its own
choices.why: An id means something in one region only.

choices.text: Its snapshots are stored and billed in us-east-1
choices.why: A copy is a separate image with separate snapshots.

choices.text: Deregistering the original removes the copy
choices.why: The copy stays.

choices.text: A fix to the original reaches the copy
choices.why: Nothing links them; fix both, or copy again.

choices.text: The copy can be encrypted with a key named at copy time
choices.why: --encrypted --kms-key-id does it.

prompt: A launch template names an image that was deregistered last week. When does somebody find out?

choices.text: At the moment the image was deregistered, by an error
choices.why: Deregistering checks nothing that refers to the image.

choices.text: Never, since the template keeps a copy of the image
choices.why: A template holds the id, not the image.

choices.text: When the running instances are stopped by AWS
choices.why: Running instances carry on; their volumes already exist.

choices.text: Only at the next launch from it, such as a scale-out
choices.why: Right, which is usually the moment the extra machine was needed.

prompt: Put the retirement of an old image in order.
hint: The snapshot ids live in the mapping, which goes with the image.
items: Move the launch templates to the newer image
Read the snapshot ids from the image's mapping
trap: Deleting the snapshots first is refused while the image is registered, and deregistering before reading the mapping loses the ids.

prompt: A weekly snapshot is kept for 52 weeks. The volume had 50 GB written at the first one, and 5 GB change each week. At 0.068 USD per GB-month, what do the 52 snapshots cost a month, in USD, to the cent?
